To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
no till soil consistently has higher volumetric water contents in the 0.0 to 1 2 m depth than plowed soil, except in late autumn or early spring when recharge takes place.
soil water storage and infiltration are greater under no tillage than under moldboard plowing in the Southern Great Plains.
no till winter wheat production systems are more effective in storing water and increasing infiltration than are conventional tillage systems.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of tillage and residue on water storage in the soil profile, which is critical to winter wheat production in the southern Great Plains.
the effects of soil tillage systems on soil water storage and infiltration.
the effects of tillage and winter wheat residue on soil water storage.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
no tillage is a better management option than plowed tillage for water storage in winter wheat production in the southern Great Plains.
no tillage system is more effective in conserving soil water than plowing, and the difference is greater in the Renfrow soil than in the Bethany soil, and the difference increases with time.
no till soil management increased soil water storage and infiltration rate in the field.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

tillage and residue practices significantly influence soil water storage, infiltration, and macropore formation, which are important factors in determining the sustainability of winter wheat production in the southern Great Plains.
no till soil management was the best practice to conserve water in the soil, and to improve soil physical properties in winter wheat cropping systems in southern Great Plains.
soil water storage was significantly increased under no till winter wheat production.
The main takeaway from our work is that
no till management can be used to enhance water storage and improve soil quality in winter wheat production in the southern Great Plains.
soil management practices can affect water storage and water infiltration, and that these effects can be long lasting.
the soil management effects on water storage are not static but dynamic, changing with the seasons.
